What is semantic HTML and why does it matter?

Semantic HTML uses elements that describe their meaning — <nav>, <main>, <article>, <button> — rather than generic <div>s. It improves accessibility (screen readers expose landmarks and roles), SEO (search engines understand structure) and maintainability. Native elements also come with built-in keyboard behaviour; a <button> is focusable and activates on Enter/Space for free.
When should you use ARIA attributes?

Only when native HTML cannot express the semantics — e.g. custom widgets like tabs (role="tablist", aria-selected), expandable panels (aria-expanded), live regions for async messages (aria-live="polite") or icon-only buttons (aria-label). ARIA changes only what assistive tech announces; it does not add behaviour, so you must also handle keyboard interaction. Incorrect ARIA is worse than none. 💡 Prefer <button> over <div role="button" tabindex="0">.
Explain the CSS box model and box-sizing.

Each element is content surrounded by padding, border and margin. With content-box (default), width: 200px plus padding: 20px and a 1px border renders 242px wide. With border-box, the total stays 200px and the content shrinks. Most projects (and Bootstrap) apply border-box to all elements for predictable sizing.
How is CSS specificity calculated?

As a tuple (IDs, classes/attributes/pseudo-classes, elements/pseudo-elements), compared left to right. #main .btn:hover = (1,2,0) beats .nav .btn.primary = (0,3,0). Inline styles beat any selector, !important overrides normal declarations, and if specificity is equal the later rule wins. 💡 Keep specificity low and flat (single classes, BEM) so overrides stay easy.
Flexbox vs Grid — when do you use each?

Flexbox is one-dimensional and content-out: great for aligning items in a row or column, like a navbar or button group. Grid is two-dimensional and layout-in: you define rows and columns and place items, ideal for page layouts and card galleries. They combine well — a grid page layout whose cells use flex to align their contents.

Difference between position relative, absolute, fixed and sticky?

relative offsets the element from its normal position but keeps its space in the flow. absolute removes it from flow and positions it relative to the nearest positioned ancestor (or the initial containing block). fixed positions relative to the viewport and stays during scroll. sticky behaves like relative until a scroll offset is reached, then sticks within its parent — commonly used for table headers.
Why does my z-index not work?

Usually because of stacking contexts. z-index only compares siblings within the same stacking context, and properties like transform, opacity < 1, filter or a positioned parent with a z-index create a new one. A child can never escape above its parent's context. Also, z-index has no effect on position: static elements (except flex/grid items). 💡 Render modals and overlays at the end of body (Angular CDK overlay does this).
What is mobile-first design?

You write base CSS for the smallest screens and add min-width media queries to progressively enhance for larger screens. It keeps mobile CSS lean, forces content prioritisation and matches how Bootstrap's breakpoints work (.col-md-6 applies from md upward). The opposite, desktop-first, uses max-width queries to undo styles.
rem vs em vs px vs %?

px is fixed. rem is relative to the root (html) font size — consistent and respects the user's browser font setting, so it is preferred for font sizes and spacing. em is relative to the current element's font size and compounds when nested, useful for padding that should scale with a button's text. % is relative to the parent's corresponding dimension; vw/vh to the viewport.
CSS custom properties vs Sass variables?

Sass variables ($brand) are resolved at compile time and disappear from the output — they cannot change at runtime. CSS custom properties (--brand) live in the browser, cascade and inherit, can be scoped to a selector or media query and updated from JavaScript. Use Sass variables for build-time configuration and custom properties for theming such as dark mode.
Which CSS properties should you animate for performance and why?

transform and opacity. The rendering pipeline is style → layout → paint → composite; these two can be handled in the composite step on the GPU, while properties like width, height, top or margin force layout recalculation and repaint every frame, causing jank. Use translate instead of left, and scale instead of changing width.
What are mixins, partials and @use in SCSS?

A partial is a file prefixed with _ that is only meant to be included, not compiled alone. A mixin is a reusable block of declarations, optionally with parameters and @content, inserted with @include. @use loads a module once with a namespace (@use "mixins" as m; then m.respond(md)), replacing the deprecated @import which caused global name collisions and duplicated output.
Mixin vs @extend vs function in Sass?

A mixin copies its declarations into every place it is included and accepts arguments. @extend makes a selector share another selector's rules by grouping selectors in the output — smaller CSS, but can produce surprising selector chains and does not work across media queries. A function returns a value (e.g. converting px to rem) rather than declarations. Prefer mixins for parameterised styles and functions for calculations.
Explain the Bootstrap 5 grid system.

It is a 12-column flexbox grid: .container (or .container-fluid) holds .rows, and rows hold .cols. Column classes are mobile-first: .col-12 .col-md-6 .col-lg-4 means full width on phones, half from 768px, a third from 992px. Gutters are set with .g-*, .gx-*, .gy-*; .col without a number shares space equally, and .offset-* / .order-* adjust placement.
How do you customise Bootstrap's theme?

Install Bootstrap via npm and import its Sass source instead of the compiled CSS. Override variables such as $primary, $font-family-base or $grid-breakpoints before the import, and optionally import only the parts you need to reduce bundle size. In Bootstrap 5.3 you can also override CSS variables at runtime (--bs-primary, component-level --bs-btn-bg) and use data-bs-theme="dark" for colour modes. 💡 Avoid editing files inside node_modules.
What is margin collapsing?

When vertical margins of adjacent block elements (or a parent and its first/last child with no padding/border between) touch, they combine into a single margin equal to the larger value rather than their sum. It only happens vertically and in normal block flow — not in flex or grid containers, or with floated/absolutely positioned elements. Adding padding, a border or using display: flow-root on the parent prevents it.
display: none vs visibility: hidden vs opacity: 0?

display: none removes the element from layout and from the accessibility tree. visibility: hidden keeps its space but hides it from view, clicks and screen readers. opacity: 0 keeps space and it is still clickable and announced, which can trap keyboard users on invisible buttons. To hide text visually but keep it for screen readers, use a "visually hidden" utility class (Bootstrap's .visually-hidden, Tailwind's sr-only).
Pseudo-class vs pseudo-element?

A pseudo-class (single colon) selects an existing element in a particular state: :hover, :focus-visible, :nth-child(2n), :checked, :has(). A pseudo-element (double colon) styles a part of an element or inserts generated content: ::before, ::after, ::placeholder, ::first-line, ::selection. ::before and ::after need a content property to render.
Media queries vs container queries: when do you use each?

Use media queries for page-level layout decisions based on the viewport or user preferences (number of columns in the page grid, prefers-reduced-motion, prefers-color-scheme, print). Use container queries for reusable components that may be placed in containers of different widths, such as a card shown in a sidebar and in a main area. They work well together: media queries for the page shell, container queries inside components.
Tailwind vs Bootstrap: which would you choose?

Bootstrap gives ready-made, accessible-ish components and JavaScript behaviour, so it is fastest for internal tools and admin UIs where a standard look is fine. Tailwind gives a design-token system of utilities and no default look, which suits custom designs and design systems, and produces small CSS because unused classes are never generated. Common criticisms of Tailwind are long class lists in markup, solved by extracting components. Mixing both in one project usually causes conflicting resets and should be avoided.

What is :focus-visible and why not just remove outlines?

:focus-visible matches when the browser decides a focus ring should be shown, which is typically keyboard navigation and not mouse clicks. Writing outline: none on :focus makes the site unusable for keyboard users and fails WCAG. Instead, style :focus-visible with a clear ring and leave mouse clicks quiet. Also add a skip link ("Skip to main content") as the first focusable element so keyboard users can bypass the navigation.
What is a BFC and when have you needed one?

A block formatting context is an independent layout box. Creating one on a parent makes it contain its floats (so its height includes floated children), stops margin collapsing between it and its children, and stops it overlapping a neighbouring float. The clean way is display: flow-root; older code used overflow: hidden or a clearfix. With flexbox and grid it is needed less often, but it explains many "why is my container height zero" bugs.
What happens if you leave out the DOCTYPE or the viewport meta tag?

Without <!DOCTYPE html>, browsers render in quirks mode, which emulates old browser bugs (for example a different box model for some elements and odd table sizing), so layouts break unpredictably. Without the viewport meta tag, mobile browsers render the page at a desktop width of about 980px and zoom out, so your media queries for small screens never match and text is tiny.
Why use the native <dialog> element instead of a div modal?

showModal() renders the dialog in the browser's top layer above everything, so no z-index or stacking-context problems; it makes the rest of the page inert, closes on Escape, moves focus into the dialog and returns it on close, and exposes the right role to screen readers. A div modal needs all of that coded by hand. Use <form method="dialog"> inside it to close with a button value.
section vs article vs aside vs div: which element do you choose?

Element | Meaning | Test to apply | Example
article | Self-contained content | Would it make sense on its own, e.g. in a feed? | A blog post, a patient note card
section | A themed group of content, usually with a heading | Would it appear in the page outline? | "Medications" and "Allergies" parts of a chart
aside | Content related to, but separate from, the main content | Could you remove it without losing the main message? | Sidebar, related links, call-out
div | No meaning at all | Only needed for styling or layout? | Flex or grid wrapper
Rule of thumb: if no semantic element fits, use a div; a wrong semantic element is worse than a neutral one. Give a section a heading.
button vs a vs div with a click handler?

| <button> | <a href> | <div (click)>
Purpose | Performs an action | Navigates to a URL | None
Keyboard focus | Yes | Yes (with href) | No, needs tabindex="0"
Activated by | Enter and Space | Enter | Nothing until you add key handlers
Screen reader role | button | link | None, needs role="button"
Inside a form | Default type is submit | Not a form control | Not a form control
Rule of thumb: "does it change the URL?" means a link; anything else is a button. Add type="button" to buttons inside forms that should not submit.
Plain script vs async vs defer vs type="module"?

| <script> | async | defer | type="module"
Blocks HTML parsing | Yes, while downloading and running | Only while running | No | No (deferred by default)
Runs when | Immediately | As soon as downloaded | After parsing, before DOMContentLoaded | Like defer (unless async is added)
Order kept | Yes | No | Yes | Yes
Good for | Rarely needed | Independent scripts, e.g. analytics | App scripts that need the DOM | Modern ES modules
Rule of thumb: use defer for your own scripts and async only for scripts that depend on nothing and nothing depends on.
:is() vs :where() vs :has()?

| :is() | :where() | :has()
What it does | Matches any selector in the list | Matches any selector in the list | Matches an element that contains (or is followed by) a match
Specificity | That of its most specific argument | Always zero | That of its most specific argument
Typical use | Shorten long selector lists | Defaults that are easy to override | Style a parent based on its children
Example | :is(h1, h2) a | :where(ul, ol) { margin: 0 } | .field:has(input:invalid)
Interview tip: :where() is the tool for library or reset styles, because any later rule can override it without a specificity fight.
CSS transition vs @keyframes animation vs JavaScript animation?

| transition | @keyframes animation | JavaScript
Trigger | A property value changes (hover, class) | Starts when applied, can run on load | Your code
Steps | Start and end only | Any number of keyframes | Anything
Loops | No | Yes (animation-iteration-count) | Yes
Control | Minimal | Pause via animation-play-state | Full: pause, reverse, seek, react to input
Good for | Hover and state changes | Spinners, attention effects | Drag, physics, scroll-linked logic
Rule of thumb: start with a transition, move to keyframes when you need more than two states, and use JavaScript only when the motion depends on user input. Respect prefers-reduced-motion in all three.
